mappings.note: When nylon was first prepared is the story of an invention, which is the only outcome in the frame covering the history of science. Not LO-1, because no property of the fibre is at issue.
Picking the plant-derived natural fibre turns on the natural versus human-made distinction LO-1 names verbatim. Not LO-2, reserved here for sorting plastics into classes.
Naming the glucose polymer, cellulose, is structural knowledge of a natural material. Not LO-2, since one substance is named rather than a class assigned.
Monomers as the repeating units of a polymer is the structure of human-made materials. Not LO-12, because no use or application follows.
Acrylic as artificial wool differentiates a synthetic fibre from its natural counterpart. Not LO-12, because the item names the fibre rather than choosing it for a job.
Rayon as the other name for artificial silk is the natural-versus-human-made comparison again. Not LO-11, since no discovery story is told.
Teflon on frying pans is choosing the right material for an everyday object, the application outcome. Not LO-1, which covers what the material is rather than where it is used.
Recognising a blended fabric as a mixture of two fibres rests on fibre identity. Not LO-2, which is used here for the thermoplastic/thermosetting classes.
Nylon for parachutes is selecting a material for a demanding use, parallel to choosing appropriate metals and non-metals in LO-12. Not LO-1, because no two fibres are compared.
Weighing nylon against rayon compares two materials on their properties, exactly LO-1. Not LO-12, since no particular application is chosen.
Choosing the fire-resistant plastic for firefighters' uniforms is an application decision. Not LO-2, because the item names a use rather than a polymer class.
Selecting the plastic for electrical switches applies material properties to a real object. Not LO-2, which fits the bare thermosetting-versus-thermoplastic sorting items.
Terylene as a form of polyester identifies a material by its composition. Not LO-2, because a trade name is matched to a substance, not a class judged.
Finding the group containing only synthetic fibres rests on telling human-made from natural, LO-1's own example. Not LO-2, which would apply to plastic classes.
Why pickles are kept in plastic, because it does not react, is applying a material property to a household choice. Not LO-4, because no phenomenon is being traced to a cause.
Placing PET in the polyester class is classification of materials by their properties. Not LO-1, because a class is assigned rather than two materials contrasted.
Nylon as the first fully synthetic fibre turns on the synthetic-versus-natural distinction. Not LO-11, which was used for the item asking when nylon was invented.
What a polyester is composed of is structural knowledge about a polymer. Not LO-2, since no classification is required.
Excluding the material that is not man-made is the natural/human-made differentiation. Not LO-12, because no use is involved.
The strongest synthetic fibre ranks materials by a property. Not LO-12, which fits the parachute item where that strength is put to use.
Wood pulp yielding rayon identifies a fibre by its natural source, the semi-synthetic case of the natural/human-made contrast. Not LO-12, because no application is chosen.
Picking the natural fibre is the core natural-versus-human-made differentiation. Not LO-2, reserved here for plastic classes.
Placing melamine among thermosetting, fire-resistant plastics is classification by property. Not LO-12, which was used for the firefighter-uniform item where the same plastic is chosen for a job.
Factory-produced fibre being called synthetic is the human-made side of LO-1's distinction. Not LO-11, since no discovery is involved.
Identifying what class PET belongs to is classification of a material by property. Not LO-1, because no contrast with another material is drawn.

Knowing which plastic cannot be recycled rests on the thermosetting/thermoplastic classification. Not LO-12, which is reserved here for the biodegradability item, where waste segregation is named verbatim in the outcome.
The non-recyclable plastic is again the thermosetting class. Same reasoning as the preceding item, which it duplicates.
Bakelite as an example of a thermosetting plastic is class assignment by property. Not LO-12, because no use of bakelite is chosen here.
Picking the non-biodegradable material is the waste-segregation application LO-12 names word for word. Not LO-2, because the point is what to do with the waste, not which polymer class it belongs to.
A duplicate of the nylon-invention item; the history-of-discovery outcome applies for the same reason. Not LO-1, since no property is tested.
What synthetic fibres are, man-made polymers, is the human-made side of LO-1. Not LO-2, because no class is being assigned within them.
Identifying a thermoplastic from linear monomer arrangement and typical products is classification from given properties. Not LO-1, because no second material is contrasted.
The synthetic fibre resembling wool is the human-made counterpart of a natural fibre. Not LO-12, since no use is chosen.
Nylon's advantage over rayon compares two materials on their properties. Duplicate of an earlier item and coded the same way.
Which everyday article is not made from high-density polythene tests where the material is actually used. Not LO-2, because no polymer class is judged.
Rayon resembling silk and called artificial silk is the natural-versus-human-made comparison. Duplicate in substance of the artificial-silk item above.
Naming the polymer coating cookware and iron soles applies material properties to household objects. Not LO-1, because the point is the use rather than the contrast.
Selecting the thermosetting plastic is direct classification of materials by property. Not LO-12, because no application follows.
Defining petrochemicals as substances derived from petroleum and natural gas places materials by their origin. Not LO-1, because no two materials are being told apart.
